::: {.lead}
Omar wants to copy the levels of *Pocket Quest* to a USB stick, and Windows
says "File too large". The stick has 16 GB free, and the file is only 5 GB.
Another player has a new gamepad that the game does not see. Both problems
come from a part of the operating system that most players never see: the
**file system** and the management of **devices**. In lecture 5 you saw how
the OS shares the CPU and the RAM. In this lesson you see how it keeps files
on a drive, how it manages devices and the other resources that games
share, and how a tester makes a phone ready for a test. Every section ends
with a short task.
:::

## Key terms

{{< glossary file-system file-path file-extension file-metadata file-system-format system-resources device-driver plug-and-play usb-mode >}}

## 6.1 Where does a game keep its files?

A game is not one file. *Pocket Quest* on Windows has a program file, packs
of levels and music, and the save files of the player. The **file system**
keeps all of them in folders, and finds them by their **path** (@fig-files).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 6.1 — File system"}
The **file system** is the part of the OS that keeps files and folders on a
drive: their names, their places (paths), their sizes and their dates. The
data about a file (name, type, size, dates, permissions) is its
**metadata**.
:::

![The files of Pocket Quest on a Windows PC: the game folder, and the save files in the player's Documents.](images/game-files.png){#fig-files width=96%}

The **file extension** (.exe, .pak, .sav, .png) tells the OS and the player
what kind of file it is. A path like
`C:\Games\PocketQuest\Data\levels.pak` goes from the drive (C:) one folder
deeper at every `\`. Android and macOS write `/` instead of `\`.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 6.1 — Game files and player files"}
1. The game folder `C:\Games\PocketQuest` holds the program (80 MB) and the
   packs `levels.pak` (1.2 GB) and `music.pak` (320 MB). They are the same
   for every player.
2. The save file `slot1.sav` (2 KB) is in the player's own folder
   `C:\Users\Omar\Documents\PocketQuest\Saves`. It is different for every
   player.
3. When Omar reinstalls the game, the game folder is new, but his save file
   stays.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Example 6.2 — The same game on a phone"}
On a phone, each app has its own folder in its sandbox (Seminar 5). The
player cannot open it; Settings shows only the size: app, user data and
cache (lecture 2).
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
"The stick has 16 GB free, so the 5 GB file fits." Not on a stick formatted
**FAT32**: it refuses any file of 4 GB or more. A stick formatted **exFAT**
takes big files and works on Windows and Mac.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Looking for the save file in the game folder. Many PC games keep the
player's files in Documents or in a hidden AppData folder, so that they stay
when the game is updated.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · The files of an app"}
On the lab computer, open File Explorer and go to `C:\Program Files`.

1. Open the folder of one program. Write the path, and the name and size of
   its biggest file.
2. Right-click the file › Properties. Write three items of its metadata.

*Your result:* one path, one file with its size, and three items of metadata.

::: {.check}
A good answer: "C:\Program Files\Mozilla Firefox, biggest file xul.dll
(140 MB)", with three items of metadata from Properties, for example the
type, the size and the date it was created.
:::
:::

## 6.2 Sharing the hardware: devices and resources

A gamepad, a headset, a camera and a USB cable are **devices**. The OS finds
them, loads their **drivers**, shares them between apps and checks
permissions. It also shares the other **resources**: CPU time, memory,
storage, battery and network (@fig-devices).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 6.2 — Device management"}
**Device management** is the job of the OS that finds connected devices
(**plug and play**), loads a **driver** for each one, gives apps access to
them in turn, and checks their permissions. The **system resources** that
the OS shares are CPU time, memory, storage, battery, network and devices.
:::

![A new gamepad: connect, detect, driver, ready. A phone asks what its USB cable may do.](images/device-management.png){#fig-devices width=96%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 6.3 — A new gamepad"}
1. Ali connects the gamepad by USB. Windows detects it and loads a driver.
2. Device Manager shows it under Human Interface Devices. If it has a yellow
   warning sign, the driver is missing.
3. With a working driver, the game reads the buttons through the OS.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Example 6.4 — A phone on a USB cable"}
1. A phone connected to a PC charges, but the PC shows no files.
2. The phone shows a USB mode: charging only, file transfer or photos.
3. Choosing **file transfer** lets the PC see the phone's folders. An iPhone
   asks "Trust this computer?" first.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Blaming the game when a device does not work. If the OS does not see the
device, no game can use it: check the connection, the driver and the
permission first.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Connect your phone"}
Connect your phone to the lab computer with a USB cable.

1. What does the PC show? Change the USB mode on the phone to file transfer
   (iPhone: tap Trust).
2. In File Explorer, find the phone's folder of photos (Android: DCIM).

*Your result:* the USB modes your phone offers and the path of the photos.

::: {.check}
After you choose file transfer (or tap Trust), the phone appears in File
Explorer under This PC. The photos are in the DCIM folder.
:::
:::

## 6.3 Making a device ready for a test

A test shows how the game runs. If the phone is full, low on battery or busy
with other apps, the test shows those problems instead. So a tester checks
the device first (@fig-check).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 6.3 — The device check"}
Before a test, check the **resources** of the **test device**: at least 2 GB
free storage; battery above 50 % or charging; only the game open; Do not
disturb on; and the OS version written in the report.
:::

![The device check, with the state of phone P5 before the test.](images/device-check.png){#fig-check width=96%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 6.5 — Freeing space on Lina's phone"}
Lina's test phone has 1.4 GB free; the test needs 2 GB.

1. She deletes two old videos (1.0 GB) after copying them to the PC.
2. She clears the cache of two apps (0.5 GB). She does **not** clear their
   storage (data): that would delete their logins and progress (lecture 2).
3. Free now: 1.4 + 1.0 + 0.5 = 2.9 GB.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Example 6.6 — Battery and apps"}
1. The battery shows 40 %. Many phones save power below about 20 %, and the
   game slows down. Lina charges to 60 % first.
2. Six apps are open. They use RAM and CPU (lecture 5). She closes them.
3. She turns on Do not disturb, so no call stops the test.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Testing with the best phone, fully charged, on the desk only. A device check
makes a test fair; it does not hide the weak phones (Seminar 4).
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Your phone's resources"}
Fill the five lines of the device check (@fig-check) for your own phone.

1. Write the value of each line now.
2. Fix one line that is "not ready" (for example clear one cache or close
   the open apps), and write the new value.

*Your result:* a filled device check with one fixed line.

::: {.check}
A good answer has the value of each line, for example "12 GB free, 46 %, 7
apps open, Do not disturb off, Android 14", and one fixed line with its new
value, for example "closed the apps: only the game is open".
:::
:::

## Case study: Disk Doctor at Byte Bay

The team of *Byte Bay* collects problems of *Pocket Quest*: Omar's FAT32
stick refuses the 5 GB `levels.pak`; Omar cannot find `slot1.sav`; Lina's
phone charges but shows no files on the PC; a test phone has 0.8 GB free;
Ali's gamepad shows a yellow sign; a 6 GB build must go on a stick for
Windows and Mac. The Game challenge of the interactive page uses these
problems. In the mini-game below you choose the fix for each one.

Support, "Update drivers manually in Windows".

## Exercises

1. What does a file system do? What is the metadata of a file?
2. Write the path of `slot1.sav` in Omar's Documents folder.
3. Why does a PC game keep the save file outside the game folder?
4. Why can a FAT32 stick not take a 5 GB file? Which format can?
5. What is a device driver? What does a yellow sign in Device Manager mean?
6. A phone charges on the PC, but the PC shows no files. What do you change?
7. Name four system resources that the OS shares between apps.
8. Name the five lines of the device check.
9. A phone has 1.2 GB free, old videos of 0.6 GB and caches of 0.3 GB. Is it
   ready after deleting the videos and clearing the caches?

## Answers to the exercises

::: {.answers}
1. It keeps files and folders on a drive with their names, paths, sizes and dates; metadata is data about a file (name, type, size, dates, permissions).
2. `C:\Users\Omar\Documents\PocketQuest\Saves\slot1.sav`.
3. So that it stays when the game is updated or reinstalled.
4. FAT32 allows no file of 4 GB or more; exFAT can.
5. A small program that lets the OS control one kind of hardware; the driver is missing or does not work.
6. The USB mode on the phone: file transfer.
7. For example CPU time, memory, storage, battery, network, devices.
8. 2 GB free; battery above 50 % or charging; only the game open; Do not disturb; the OS version in the report.
9. 1.2 + 0.6 + 0.3 = 2.1 GB: yes, more than 2 GB.
:::
